html:
A prehistoric mound near the Bang Pakong River in Chonburi province, Thailand, lived in and used for burials from about 2000 to 1500 BCE. It holds some of the earliest evidence of rice on the Southeast Asian mainland.

The site was dug in 1984 and 1985 by Charles Higham and Rachanie Thosarat. They found about 150 burials in seven phases, laid out in family groups over many generations. The people lived by an estuary and ate mostly fish and shellfish. Rice husks show up in pottery and in the remains of meals; whether the people grew it themselves or traded for it is still argued.

The best known grave is that of a woman buried with tens of thousands of shell beads and pottery tools, nicknamed the Princess of Khok Phanom Di. She was probably a master potter. The site fits the spread of rice farming south from China that is linked with Austroasiatic speaking peoples, and it comes before the bronze age villages of Ban Chiang.
sum: A prehistoric mound near the Bang Pakong River in Chonburi province, Thailand, lived in and used for burials from about 2000 to 1500 BCE. It holds some of the earliest evidence of rice on the Southeast Asian mainland.
